paper_title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) are increasingly expected to assist users while observing continuous audiovisual streams. However, existing evaluations provide limited insight into how reliably these models connect stream evidence and user needs to timely, sustained interventions. We introduce \textbf{Omni-InteractScope}, a benchmark of 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets across eight task groups. It links input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs, covering event-timed tool invocation and query-free assistance alongside notifications, warnings, state tracking, and continuous responses. Our experimental results on the proposed benchmark reveal three critical limitations of current Omni-LLMs: (1) \textbf{Timely tool invocation remains unreliable}: all 12 evaluated models produce an on-time first response for at most 40\% of tool-invocation targets, and joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0\%. (2) \textbf{Query-free reminders remain poorly covered}: all evaluated models achieve lower timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders than on explicit questions, measured on their respective target sets. Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0\%. (3) \textbf{End-to-end guidance coverage remains limited}: nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and the remaining three cover only one to three sequences each. Targeted controls further show that tool-invocation scores alone do not establish event grounding and that reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency. These findings motivate developing and evaluating streaming assistants for timely action, initiative under general user needs, and coverage of entire response sequences.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) such as GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-Omni, and Qwen3Omni bring joint audiovisual understanding into conversational systems (Hurst et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025a;b). Emerging streaming systems extend this ability to deciding when to speak, remain silent, or invoke tools (Chen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026b; ByteDance Seed, 2026). For an assistant observing changing environment, these decisions must serve users ongoing needs: retrieve information when requested event occurs, relay relevant sound to user with hearing impairment, or provide continue guidance as an activity unfolds (see Figure 1). Useful assistance therefore requires connecting perceptual evidence to what intervention is needed, when it is useful, and whether further responses remain necessary. Evaluation has progressed from video comprehension toward interactive assistance. Early works, such as Video-MME and LongVideoBench, assess understanding of supplied videos (Fu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024), while StreamingBench and OVO-Bench restrict observations to available stream Corresponding author.

Interactions with multiple targets record the responses required after an initial answer. This organization supports evaluating both individual interventions and coverage of continuing obligations within shared resource. Within this broad coverage, we focus on two complementary demands of proactive interaction. Tool invocation requires selecting the appropriate tool and acting when user-specified event occurs. Query-free assistance requires recognizing when general user need warrants reminder without an event-specific query. Paired controls examine the roles of scene evidence and response policy, while successive targets assess whether the assistant delivers the further responses required as an interaction unfolds. Evaluation across 12 models reveals substantial limitations in both timely intervention and sustained assistance. Every evaluated model produces an on-time first response for at most 40% of toolinvocation targets, and joint accuracy reaches at most 32.0%. Timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders never exceeds 23.0%. Although guidance-step recall reaches 51.7%, nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and no model covers more than three. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce Omni-InteractScope, comprehensive benchmark for timely and sustained omnimodal intervention. It comprises 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions across eight task groups, with 1,790 targets specifying what to produce and when, including successive responses under continuing user needs. We provide focused evaluation of event-timed action and query-free initiative through 200 tool-invocation targets and 122 query-free reminders. Our diagnostics distinguish tool choice from timing and test whether invocation scores depend on scene evidence. Paired controls further examine how explicit event cues, response scheduling, history, and response frequency affect coverage on the same reminder targets. We perform comprehensive evaluation of 12 multimodal models, providing empirical insights into timing, query-free assistance, and sequence coverage, exposing gaps between tool selection and timely action, question answering, and query-free reminders, and step coverage and complete guidance.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: From video understanding to proactive interaction. Video-MME and LongVideoBench evaluate comprehension of supplied videos (Fu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024). StreamingBench and OVO-Bench restrict observations to available stream prefixes and test responses to unfolding events (Lin et al., 2026; Niu et al., 2025). OmniMMI and OmniPro extend evaluation to multimodal interaction and audio-dependent proactivity (Wang et al., 2025b; Zhao et al., 2026). IPIBench studies evolving requests, while OmniInteract evaluates turn-taking, interruption, and recovery (Li et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026b). These works motivate causal evaluation of response content and timing. Omni-InteractScope records the intervention required by user need, including targets that remain after an initial response. Tool use and continuing response obligations. ToolBench and API-Bank evaluate tool-use plans and executable calls (Qin et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023). StreamArena brings tool utilization and proactivity into hour-scale causal streams, including external search and answer integration (Zhang et al., 2026). Our event-timed tool invocation (T1) setting evaluates tool identity and invocation timing, with controls that distinguish request priors from scene evidence. Omni-DuplexEval includes continuous descriptions and event-conditioned reminders, and OmniAssistBench evaluates assistance along predefined paths (He et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). We retain successive targets within each interaction and report both individual-target and complete-guidance coverage. sections.title: 3 OMNI-INTERACTSCOPE
sections.content: Omni-InteractScope comprises 1,479 interactions across eight task groups, organized around the interventions an assistant should deliver as stream unfolds. Figure 1 summarizes the design, and Figure 2 illustrates each task group in details.

sections.title: 3.1 DESIGNING FOR TIMELY AND SUSTAINED INTERVENTION
sections.content: The benchmark unit is an interaction: video and audio stream, user context, and one or more reference interventions. Each intervention is target specifying the required response and its reference time or valid interval. For continuing request, the interaction retains successive targets in temporal order. We organize this unit along four linked dimensions. Input modalities describe the available video, scene audio, and user context conveyed through text, speech, or image attachments. Event triggers describe the evidence or condition associated with response, such as an object appearing, sound, an accumulated count, or elapsed time. Intervention types specify what the assistant should produce: an answer, notification, warning, tool call, or successive commentary or guidance. User needs determine why that intervention matters, through an explicit request or general visualor hearing-assistance instruction. Together, these dimensions connect stream evidence and user context to the interventions an assistant should provide. The eight task groups organize these requirements into comprehensive evaluation of response content, timing, and coverage, encompassing both individual interventions and successive responses under continuing user needs.

sections.title: 3.3 DATA CONSTRUCTION AND ANNOTATION
sections.content: The benchmark combines 905 online video records for explicit-request tasks with 207 self-recorded first-person video records for impairment assistance. It spans indoor, outdoor, and digital-screen settings, with QA text approximately balanced between English and Chinese (744 and 735 interactions, respectively). The 1,479 interactions contain 1,790 targets, with multiple targets in 163 interactions. Appendix details task counts, scene and trigger distributions, duration statistics, and source provenance, including repeated source identities among video records. Human annotators specified user context, reference responses, triggers, and response times or valid intervals. separate group of human reviewers cross-checked the annotations to obtain the final benchmark. This review covers both response content and its temporal relation to the event. Appendix A.4 documents the supplemental consistency audit and review records.

sections.content: Tables 2 and 3 report explicit-request and assistance results. Avg. equally weights T1T4, T6, and T7, with T5 reported separately. Assistance results pool target recall and count complete guidance sequences. Configurations differ in inputs and execution interfaces (Appendix D.4.1 examines within-model schedule effects). After media-validity exclusions, evaluation covers 1,477 interactions and 1,788 targets (Appendix A.1). Task strengths vary across intervention types. Gemini-3.5-Flash leads the six-task Avg., while Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus leads tool invocation. Yet the best scores on cumulative-state tracking (T4) and continuous responses (T7) are only 11.2% and 11.4%, respectively. These weaknesses span both timing and content: Gemini-3.5-Flash responds prematurely on 172/206 T4 targets, while its T7 failures include 233/457 premature responses and 152/457 timely content failures (Appendix D.4.3). Task-level and failure breakdowns therefore reveal limitations obscured by the aggregate ranking. Reminder coverage is lower than question coverage. Every configuration covers smaller fraction of query-free reminders (T8-A) than explicit questions (T8-B). Even Gemini-3.1-Pro, which leads both, reaches 23.0% on reminders versus 62.3% on questions. Gemini-3.1-Pro covers 51.7% of T8-C steps but completes only 3 of 26 guidance sequences. No open-source prompted or streaming configuration completes sequence. Complete T8-C measures coverage of the annotated trajectory, not closed-loop user-task success. Section 5.3 relates completion to individual-step coverage.

sections.title: 5.1 SCENE EVIDENCE AND TOOL-INVOCATION SCORES
sections.content: Figure 3a shows that removing scene input does not lower Gemini-3.5-Flashs T1 accuracy. On the same 200 interactions, joint accuracy is 29.50% with scene input and 33.00% without it, with requests and the evaluation protocol held fixed. The paired difference is 3.50 percentage points. Joint accuracy alone therefore does not establish event-grounded invocation. Appendices D.1.2 and D.4.2 detail the paired ablation and temporal-tolerance analysis. The request-only control reveals strong task priors. Gemini-3.5-Flash selects 96.5% of tools from request text and public definitions alone. Emitting these choices after fixed three-second delay gives 68.0% joint success, the highest of four tested delays. This separate control uses closedlabel output interface and different response opportunities from the main evaluation, so it diagnoses request and timing priors rather than providing matched model ranking (Appendix D.1.1).

sections.title: 5.2 REMINDER COVERAGE UNDER DIFFERENT RESPONSE POLICIES
sections.content: As shown in Figure 3b, giving Gemini-3.5-Flash response history reduces output volume by 58.1%, while both conditions cover 22 of 122 T8-A targets. The matched targets change, with 12 gained and 12 lost. Adding cooldown reduces outputs further but costs 9.84 percentage points of recall relative to history alone. The policy is implemented by skipping generation calls during the cooldown, restricting the opportunities to cover reminder targets (Appendix D.2.2). Figure 3c compares event-specific and general instructions in separate runs on the same 122 T8-A episodes. Gemini-3.5-Flash and Qwen2.5-Omni benefit from event cues when response is requested at an annotated valid time. Under autonomous responding, however, the effects are small and uncertain. The benefit of event cues is therefore clearer when the response time is supplied than when the model must decide when to intervene. Scheduling changes temporal information and response opportunities together, so this comparison does not isolate planning mechanism.

sections.title: 5.3 COMPLETE GUIDANCE RELATIVE TO STEP COVERAGE
sections.content: On the same 20 three-step T8-C episodes, Gemini-3.1-Pro covers 30 of 60 steps but completes only three sequences. Complete T8-C complements step recall by recording whether all required guidance was delivered.

sections.title: 6 DISCUSSION
sections.content: Invocation scores need evidence controls. The T1 controls show that request information and response timing can sustain joint success without scene inputs. tool-and-time score should therefore be accompanied by evidence controls when used to assess event grounding. For streaming tool use (Zhang et al., 2026), varying event occurrence and timing while holding requests fixed would test stronger requirement than the scene ablation evaluated here. Coverage depends on the response policy. Response history reduces Gemini-3.5-Flashs output volume with the same aggregate recall point estimate, while cooldown reduces both outputs and coverage. These findings connect response-frequency evaluation (Chatterjee et al., 2026) to the policies used during generation. Reporting history access and output rate alongside recall makes this dependence visible. Selectivity additionally requires evaluating the value and cost of interventions beyond the annotated targets, an important direction for future benchmark development. Complete coverage has separate measurement role. Users may need every guidance step even when individual responses are often correct. Complete T8-C expresses that requirement, while the sequence reference limits attribution of low completion to separate memory or planning failure. For goal-oriented assistants (Sun et al., 2026), explicit records of delivered guidance and pending obligations remain design hypothesis to test through interventions on history and state.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced Omni-InteractScope, benchmark for timely and sustained intervention in continuous omnimodal streams. Its 1,479 human-annotated interactions span eight task groups, linking user needs and stream evidence to 1,790 targets that specify response content and timing. Evaluation across 12 models reveals substantial limitations in timely tool invocation, query-free reminders, and complete guidance coverage. These findings underscore the need to assess whether assistants fulfill the response requirements of an interaction, including interventions that remain necessary after an initial answer. Omni-InteractScope provides shared basis for developing and evaluating assistants that respond to unfolding events and sustain support for continuing user needs.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools to help reorganize the benchmark task taxonomy, support translation, and improve the clarity and language of the manuscript. We also used an LLM judge for preliminary data validation prior to final human verification. Separately, LLM-based content judging was used in benchmark evaluation, as detailed in Appendix B. AI tools additionally assisted with organizing and presenting qualitative cases in Appendix E. Generative AI was not used to generate synthetic benchmark data, propose or refine research hypotheses, design the research methodology or experiments, implement the evaluated methods, or clean or reformat the benchmark dataset. It was also not used to develop theoretical models or new conceptual frameworks, formulate mathematical claims, or contribute to or write mathematical proofs. The authors retained responsibility for methodological decisions, qualitative judgments, and the scientific interpretation of the results. All benchmark media and annotations underwent rigorous human review. We take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including any text, claims, code, or other artifacts produced with the assistance of generative AI.

C.2 MODEL SIZES AND GENERATION SETTINGS MiniCPM-o 4.5 and MOSS-VL have 9B and 11.3B full-model parameters, respectively, despite both using Qwen3-8B language backbone. Proprietary parameter counts are undisclosed. Local prompted models use greedy decoding; hosted calls use temperature zero. Gemini-3.1-Pro and Gemini-3.5-Flash retain provider-default thinking, so their limits are not answer-only token budgets. MiniCPM-o 4.5 uses greedy duplex decoding, 20 spoken tokens per chunk, and 30-unit context window. LiveCC uses repetition penalty of 1.05 and resets at 28,000 tokens; MMDuet2 resets at 100,000. MOSS-VL uses greedy session generation with 512-token setting and pace of 12 tokens per second. AURA uses temperature zero and 512-token limit. Context retention and computation are not equalized across interfaces. Recorded model revisions and configuration fingerprints are retained in the reproducibility materials.
